page: Amazon Web Services t3.medium is a burstable general-purpose instance powered by the AWS Nitro System. It features an x86_64 architecture utilizing an Intel Xeon 8259CL processor running at 2.5 GHz. The hardware configuration provides 2 vCPUs derived from 1 physical core with hyper-threading enabled, alongside 4.0 GB of DDR4 memory operating at 3 GHz. This instance does not include local storage or dedicated GPU hardware, and operates with a baseline network bandwidth of 0 Gbps.

Performance benchmarks place the t3.medium in the lower tier of evaluated systems, with stress-ng single-core and multi-core CPU metrics falling into the bottom 10%. Memory bandwidth tests show a read-only cached small block speed of 72.83 GB/sec, which drops to 10.18 GB/sec for uncached large blocks. Similarly, database operations, Redis SET operations at 1.65 million operations per second, and static web serving throughput of 1.69 GB/sec reflect its resource-constrained, burstable design.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the t3.medium offers a low-cost entry point for workloads that do not require continuous high CPU utilization. The burstable CPU allocation model allows the instance to handle occasional spikes in traffic or processing demands while maintaining a low baseline cost. This makes it suitable for low-traffic web servers, small development or testing environments, code repositories, and microservices that experience intermittent activity.
description: Amazon Web Services t3.medium is a burstable, entry-level instance designed for workloads with variable CPU utilization. Running on the AWS Nitro System, it features an x86_64 Intel Xeon 8259CL processor clocked at 2.5 GHz, delivering 2 vCPUs from a single physical core. The instance is equipped with 4.0 GB of DDR4 memory but lacks local storage and dedicated GPU accelerators. Benchmark results, including stress-ng and Geekbench scores, position this instance in the lower performance tier, reflecting its budget-friendly, resource-constrained profile. The t3.medium is qualitatively cost-effective for non-intensive applications, making it highly suitable for development environments, low-traffic web servers, microservices, and small code repositories that require intermittent burst capacity rather than sustained high-performance compute.
